paragraphs: No country in the world has made more successful use of the principle of association, or applied it more freely to so many different purposes, than America. Besides the permanent associations that the law establishes under the names of townships, cities, and counties, there are a great many others that private individuals form and maintain.

From earliest childhood, the citizen of the United States is taught to rely on his own efforts to resist the evils and difficulties of life. He regards social authority with mistrust and anxiety, and he asks for its help only when he cannot possibly manage without it. One can see this habit even in the schools, where children at play follow rules they have set for themselves and punish offenses they have defined themselves. The same spirit runs through every act of social life. Suppose a blockage occurs on a public road and traffic is held up. The neighbors at once form themselves into a deliberative body, and this improvised assembly produces an executive power that removes the obstruction before anyone has thought of turning to an authority higher than the people directly concerned. If public entertainment is at stake, an association is formed to provide for its splendor and good order. Societies are formed to fight enemies of a purely moral kind and to reduce the vice of intemperance. In the United States, associations are established to promote public order, commerce, industry, morality, and religion; for there is no goal that the human will, backed by the combined efforts of individuals, despairs of reaching.

Later I shall have occasion to show what effects association has on the course of society. For the present I must limit myself to the political world. Once the right of association is recognized, citizens may use it in several different ways.

An association consists simply of the public agreement that a number of individuals give to certain doctrines, and of their commitment to promote the spread of those doctrines by their efforts. The right of association in this sense is very close to the liberty of publishing without a license, but societies formed in this way have more authority than the press. When a society represents an opinion, that opinion necessarily takes a more exact and explicit form. It counts its supporters and binds their welfare to its cause. The supporters, for their part, come to know one another, and their zeal grows with their numbers. An association brings together the efforts of minds that tend to diverge and channels them in a single direction, driving them forcefully toward the one goal that it names.

The second degree of the right of association is the power to hold meetings. When an association is allowed to set up centers of action at certain important points in the country, its activity increases and its influence spreads. People have the chance to see one another, the means of carrying out their plans are more easily combined, and opinions are held with a warmth and energy that the written word cannot match.

Finally, the exercise of the right of political association has a third degree. The supporters of an opinion may unite in electoral bodies and choose delegates to represent them in a central assembly. This is, properly speaking, the representative system applied to a party.

Thus, in the first case, a society is formed among individuals who profess the same opinion, and the tie that holds it together is purely intellectual. In the second case, small assemblies are formed that represent only a fraction of the party. In the third case, finally, the party forms a separate nation within the nation, a government within the government. Its delegates, like the true delegates of the majority, represent the whole collective force of their party, and they enjoy something of the national dignity and great influence that belong to the people’s chosen representatives. It is true that they do not have the right to make laws, but they do have the power to attack the laws that exist and to draw up in advance those that they may later get adopted.

Suppose a people is not fully accustomed to the exercise of freedom, or is exposed to violent political passions. If a deliberating minority, which confines itself to considering future laws, is set alongside the legislative majority, I cannot help believing that public tranquility runs very great risks in that nation. There is no doubt a very wide difference between proving that one law is better in itself than another and proving that the first ought to replace the second. But the imagination of the common people easily overlooks this difference, which is so plain to thoughtful minds. It sometimes happens that a nation is divided into two nearly equal parties, each of which claims to represent the majority. If another power is set up right next to the governing power, and it has almost as much moral authority, it is not to be believed that it will be content for long to speak without acting. Nor is it to be believed that it will always be held back by the abstract consideration that associations exist to guide opinion but not to enforce it, to suggest laws but not to make them.

The more we consider the independence of the press in its main consequences, the more we are convinced that it is the chief element of freedom in the modern world, and, so to speak, the one that constitutes it. A nation determined to remain free is therefore right to demand that this independence be exercised without restraint. But unrestrained liberty of political association cannot be treated as entirely the same as liberty of the press. The one is at once less necessary and more dangerous than the other. A nation may limit it without giving up any part of its self-control, and it may sometimes be obliged to do so in order to maintain its own authority.
In America the liberty of association for political purposes is unlimited. An example will show most clearly how far this privilege is tolerated.

The question of the tariff, or of free trade, produced a great display of party feeling in America. The tariff was not only a subject of debate as a matter of opinion; it also had a favorable or harmful effect on several very powerful interests of the States. The North attributed a great part of its prosperity to this system, and the South all of its sufferings. As a result, for a long time the tariff was the only source of the political animosities that agitated the Union.

In 1831, when the dispute was raging with the greatest bitterness, a private citizen of Massachusetts used the newspapers to propose that all opponents of the tariff send delegates to Philadelphia, to consult together on the means best suited to promote freedom of trade. Thanks to the power of the printing press, this proposal spread from Maine to New Orleans within a few days. The opponents of the tariff adopted it with enthusiasm, meetings were held on all sides, and delegates were named. Most of these men were well known, and some had gained considerable fame. South Carolina alone, which afterwards took up arms in the same cause, sent sixty-three delegates. On October 1, 1831, this assembly, which in the American custom had taken the name of a Convention, met at Philadelphia. It had more than two hundred members. Its debates were public, and they took on a legislative character at once. The extent of the powers of Congress, the theories of free trade, and the various clauses of the tariff were discussed in turn. After ten days of deliberation the Convention broke up, having published an address to the American people, in which it declared:
I. That Congress had not the right of making a tariff, and that the existing tariff was unconstitutional;
II. That the prohibition of free trade was prejudicial to the interests of all nations, and to that of the American people in particular.

It must be admitted that unrestrained liberty of political association has not so far produced, in the United States, the fatal consequences that one might perhaps expect from it elsewhere. The right of association was brought over from England and has always existed in America, so that the exercise of this privilege is now blended with the manners and customs of the people. At the present time the liberty of association has become a necessary guarantee against the tyranny of the majority. In the United States, as soon as a party has become dominant, all public authority passes under its control. Its private supporters fill all the offices and have the whole force of the administration at their disposal. The most distinguished supporters of the other side cannot overcome the obstacles that keep them out of power. They therefore need some means of establishing themselves on their own footing and of setting the moral authority of the minority against the physical power that dominates it. Thus a dangerous expedient is used to ward off a still more formidable danger.

The omnipotence of the majority seems to me to pose such extreme perils to the American Republics that the dangerous measure used to check it appears to do more good than harm. And here I am about to put forward a proposition that may remind the reader of what I said earlier about municipal freedom. There are no countries where associations are more needed, to prevent the despotism of faction or the arbitrary power of a prince, than those that are democratically constituted. In aristocratic nations the body of the nobles and the wealthier part of the community are themselves natural associations, which act as checks on abuses of power. In countries where such associations do not exist, if private individuals cannot create an artificial and temporary substitute for them, I can imagine no lasting protection against the most galling tyranny. A great people may then be oppressed by a small faction, or by a single individual, with impunity.

The meeting of a great political Convention (for there are Conventions of every kind) may often become a necessary measure, but it is always a serious event, even in America. The sensible friends of the country never look forward to it without alarm. This was very noticeable in the Convention of 1831, where the efforts of all the most distinguished members of the Assembly tended to moderate its language and to keep the subjects it treated within certain limits. It is probable, in fact, that the Convention of 1831 had a very great influence on the minds of the malcontents and prepared them for the open revolt against the commercial laws of the Union that took place in 1832.

No one can deny that unrestrained liberty of association for political purposes is the privilege a people learns to use last. Even when it does not plunge the nation into anarchy, it keeps raising the chances of that disaster. On one point, however, this dangerous liberty protects against a different kind of danger: where associations are free, secret societies are unknown. In America there are numerous factions, but no conspiracies.
Different Ways in Which the Right of Association Is Understood in Europe and in the United States — Different Use Made of It.

After the right of acting for himself, the most natural privilege of man is to combine his efforts with those of his fellow creatures and to act in common with them. I am therefore led to conclude that the right of association is almost as inalienable as the right of personal liberty. No legislator can attack it without damaging the very foundations of society. Nevertheless, the liberty of association is a fruitful source of advantages and prosperity for some nations, but others may pervert it or carry it to excess, and what gives life may be turned into a source of destruction. It may perhaps be thought useful, both to governments and to parties, to compare the different methods that associations follow in countries where they are managed with discretion and in those where liberty degenerates into license.

Most Europeans look upon an association as a weapon, to be hastily forged and tried out at once in the fight. A society is formed for discussion, but the idea of coming action dominates the minds of its members. It is in fact an army, and the time given to talk serves to count its strength and rouse the courage of the host, after which it marches against the enemy. The resources that lie within the bounds of the law may occur to its members as means of success, but never as the only means.

This, however, is not how the right of association is understood in the United States. In America, the citizens who make up the minority associate, first, to show their numerical strength and so to weaken the moral authority of the majority. Second, they associate to stimulate rivalry and to discover the arguments best suited to influence the majority; for they always hope to win their opponents over to their side and then to use the supreme power in their name. Political associations in the United States are therefore peaceable in their intentions and strictly legal in the means they use. They claim, with perfect truth, that they aim at success only by lawful means.

The difference between the Americans and ourselves depends on several causes. In Europe there are many parties so completely opposed to the majority that they can never hope to gain its support, and at the same time they think they are strong enough in themselves to struggle and to defend their cause. When a party of this kind forms an association, its object is not to conquer but to fight. In America, those whose opinions are far from the majority’s are no obstacle at all to its power, and all other parties hope in the end to win it over to their own principles. The exercise of the right of association becomes dangerous in proportion to how impossible it is for great parties to gain the majority. In a country like the United States, where differences of opinion are mere differences of shade, the right of association may remain unrestrained without bad consequences. Many European nations are inexperienced in the enjoyment of liberty, and this leads them to see the liberty of association only as a right to attack the government. The first idea that occurs to a party, as to an individual, once it has become conscious of its own strength, is that of violence. The idea of persuasion comes later and is learned only from experience. The English, who are divided into parties that differ most essentially from one another, rarely abuse the right of association, because they have long been used to exercising it. In France the passion for war is so intense that there is no undertaking so mad, or so harmful to the welfare of the State, that a man does not consider himself honored to defend it at the risk of his life.

But perhaps the most powerful of the causes that tend to soften the excesses of political association in the United States is universal suffrage. In countries where universal suffrage exists, the majority is never in doubt, because neither party can claim to represent the part of the community that has not voted. The associations that are formed know, as does the nation at large, that they do not represent the majority. This is indeed a condition inseparable from their existence; for if they did represent the dominant power, they would change the law instead of asking for its reform. The consequence is that the moral influence of the government they attack is greatly increased, and their own power is greatly weakened.

In Europe there are few associations that do not claim to represent the majority, or that do not believe they represent it. This conviction or this claim tends to increase their force enormously, and it contributes no less to making their measures seem legitimate. Violence may seem excusable in defense of the cause of oppressed right. Thus it is, in the vast labyrinth of human laws, that extreme liberty sometimes corrects the abuses of license, and that extreme democracy averts the dangers of democratic government. In Europe, associations regard themselves, to some degree, as the legislative and executive councils of the people, who are unable to speak for themselves. In America, where they represent only a minority of the nation, they argue and they petition.

The means that the associations of Europe use match the end they want to reach. The main aim of these bodies is to act and not to debate, to fight rather than to persuade. They are therefore naturally led to adopt a form of organization that differs from the ordinary customs of civil bodies and takes on the habits and maxims of military life. They centralize the direction of their resources as much as possible, and they entrust the power of the whole party to a very small number of leaders.

The members of these associations answer to a watchword, like soldiers on duty. They profess the doctrine of passive obedience; or rather, in uniting together they at once give up the exercise of their own judgment and free will. The tyrannical control these societies exercise is often far more unbearable than the authority that the government they attack holds over society. Such excesses greatly reduce their moral force, and they lose the powerful interest that a struggle between oppressors and oppressed always arouses. A man who in certain cases agrees to obey his fellows servilely, and who submits his activity and even his opinions to their control, can have no claim to be called a free citizen.

The Americans have also established certain forms of government for their associations, but these are invariably borrowed from the forms of civil administration. The independence of each individual is formally recognized. The members of the association tend toward the same end, as they do in the community at large, but they are not obliged to follow the same path. No one gives up the exercise of his reason and his free will, but everyone uses that reason and that will for the benefit of a common undertaking.
